etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English gele, borrowed from Old French gelee, borrowed from Early Medieval Latin gelāta, from Latin gelō + -āta. Doublet of gelee.

definitions.definition: (Commonwealth) A dessert made by boiling gelatine, sugar and some flavouring (often derived from fruit) and allowing it to set.
(chiefly Canada, US) A clear or translucent fruit preserve, made from fruit juice and set using either naturally occurring, or added, pectin.

quote.citation: 1945, Fannie Merritt Farmer and Wilma Lord Perkins (revisor), The Boston Cooking-School Cook Book, Eighth edition:
quote.text: Perfect jelly is of appetizing flavor; beautifully colored and translucent; tender enough to cut easily with a spoon, yet firm enough to hold its shape when turned from the glass.

quote.citation: 1975, Irma S. Rombauer and Marion Rombauer Becker, The Joy of Cooking, 5th revision:
quote.text: Jelly has great clarity. Two cooking processes are involved. First, the juice alone is extracted from the fruit. Only that portion thin and clear enough to drip through a cloth is cooked with sugar until sufficiently firm to hold its shape. It is never stiff and never gummy.

definitions.definition: A savoury substance, derived from meat, that has the same texture as the dessert.
Any substance or object having the consistency of jelly.

quote.text: Sam floored him perpetually, and beat his face to a jelly, without getting a scratch.

quote.citation: 1900 December – 1901 August, H[erbert] G[eorge] Wells, “chapter 24”, in The First Men in the Moon, London: George Newnes, […], published 1901, →OCLC:
quote.text: […]  some of the profounder scholars are altogether too great for locomotion, and are carried from place to place in a sort of sedan tub, wabbling jellies of knowledge that enlist my respectful astonishment.

quote.citation: 2014, Theo Tait, ‘Water-Borne Zombies’, London Review of Books, volume 36, number 5:
quote.text: Species of the phylum Cnidaria – the classic jelly – have existed in something close to their current form for at least 565 million years; Ctenophora, the comb jellies, are not much younger.

definitions.definition: (slang, now rare) A pretty girl; a girlfriend.

quote.citation: 1931, William Faulkner, Sanctuary, Vintage, published 1993, page 25:
quote.text: ‘Gowan goes to Oxford a lot,’ the boy said. ‘He′s got a jelly there.’

definitions.definition: (US, slang) A large backside, especially a woman's.

quote.text: I shake my jelly at every chance / When I whip with my hips you slip into a trance

quote.citation: 2001, George Dell, Dance Unto the Lord, page 94:
quote.text: At that Sister Samantha seemed to shake her jelly so that she sank back into her chair.

quote.citation: 2006, David L. Marcus, What It Takes to Pull Me Through:
quote.text: Mary Alice gazed at a picture of herself wearing jellies and an oversized turquoise T-shirt that matched her eyes  […]

definitions.definition: To wiggle like jelly. (Can we add an example for this sense?)

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Clipping of jealous +‎ -y (informal adjective ending).

quote.text: "I think other people make rude comments because they're jelly [jealous] bro," Schroer said. "We're just showing our love to other people."

definitions.definition: (India) Vitrified brick refuse used as metal in building roads.

quote.citation: 1862, Notes on Building and Road-making, with Rules for Estimating Repairs to Tanks and Channels, page 143:
quote.text: Under pinning with jelly in chunam — one square.
